text: Thursday, October 30th, 2014, a little after six in the evening at a defunct airfield near Tannersville in the Pocono Mountains of Pennsylvania. A team of US Marshals is working its way across the property. The state police asked them to clear this place, an abandoned resort with an old airstrip, and they've been at it for about two hours. Their commander, a marshal named Scott Malkowski, is walking toward the hangar with two members of his team when something moves at the edge of the woods. A man is coming out of the trees, heading for the hangar. Later, telling reporters about it, Malkowski kept coming back to one detail: "I saw the black hat." The marshals order him to the ground. He doesn't run, and he doesn't fight. He isn't carrying a gun. They ask him his name, and he gives them the real one: Erik Frein. For forty-eight days, he'd been the most wanted man in Pennsylvania. More than a thousand officers took part in the search at one point or another. There were roadblocks and closed schools, and a whole corner of the state was living under it, and it ends in a field next to an empty hangar. Then the marshals handed him over to the Pennsylvania State Police, and the troopers put something on him that belonged to Brian Dixon. We'll get there. First, the question underneath all of this: how did one man stay out of reach for seven weeks while one of the biggest searches in the state's history went on around him? Part of the answer is that police believed he'd been preparing for this, as they put it at the time, for months or maybe years. Everything here comes from the Pennsylvania Supreme Court's opinion in his case, trial testimony, state police and US Marshals statements, and reporting from the time. Where accounts disagree, I'll tell you. Seven weeks earlier, Friday night, September 12th, 2014. The Pennsylvania State Police barracks in Blooming Grove in Pike County has forest pressing in on almost every side. It's shortly before eleven, and it's shift change. One group of troopers is finishing up and another is arriving. Corporal Brian Dixon is one of the troopers on his way out. He's thirty-eight, from Dunmore, a Marine veteran, married with two young sons. Early accounts say he was heading toward his patrol car. Dixon had his own assigned cruiser at Blooming Grove. Hold on to that. It comes back at the end of this story. A rifle shot comes out of the dark, and Dixon goes down outside the building. Trooper Alex Douglas, thirty-one, has just arrived for his shift along with three other troopers. He carries a gym bag out to his own vehicle, hears a noise, and sees Dixon on the ground. He goes toward him, and he's shot too. Badly wounded, Douglas gets himself into the lobby. Two troopers pull him farther inside. Officers and paramedics worked on Brian Dixon, and they couldn't save him. Alex Douglas survived. He was in the hospital until the middle of October, then moved to a rehabilitation facility. By late March 2015, he said he had already been through sixteen surgeries, with another one scheduled. Weeks later, police would have a few torn notebook pages describing that night. One line is in the court record. "Got a shot around eleven PM and took it." That night, though, nobody knew who had written anything. Whoever fired those shots had disappeared into the trees. There was no suspect and no name. They didn't even have a vehicle. That changed within days. On Sunday, September fourteenth, according to the court, a man walking his dog spotted a Jeep stuck in a retention pond, sitting partly under water, and reported it to state police. The Jeep was registered to Erik Frein's parents. Inside, police found a black rifle case, two spent cartridge casings, and Erik Frein's driver's license. His own notes would later explain the Jeep. After the shooting, he'd tried to get away in it and ended up in the swamp. He called it a disaster. Then he went into the woods on foot. So within a couple of days, police had a name, a face, and an address. What they didn't have was Erik Frein. Erik Frein was thirty-one and lived with his parents in Canadensis, a small town in Barrett Township in the same part of the Poconos. He belonged to a military reenactment group, the kind of hobby where people put on uniforms and act out history. Frein's group portrayed Eastern European soldiers. During the manhunt, Lieutenant Colonel George Bivens of the state police said Frein appeared to have assumed that role in real life. Police also told reporters that Frein had talked about wanting to commit mass murder. They weren't describing a man who'd snapped one night. Police said Frein had been preparing for months, maybe years. His computer showed research on avoiding police manhunts, on law enforcement technology, and on survival. In his recorded statement after the arrest, he said he'd used Google Earth to look at state police barracks near his home and that he chose Blooming Grove because of the woods around it. Hold on to that recorded statement, by the way. Years later, Pennsylvania's highest court would say the jury should never have seen it. The search that followed was enormous. Over its seven weeks, more than a thousand officers from state police, the FBI, the US Marshals, and departments across the region took part. At one stage, police said their focus was an area of roughly five square miles of steep, wooded ground. Later, a neighborhood called Snow Hill Falls got a lot of attention, though police said they were searching other places too. For people who lived there, normal life stopped. Roads were blocked. Schools closed at times. Local businesses lost money as visitors stayed away. And in Barrett Township, door-to-door trick-or-treating was canceled for Halloween. Remember that. It comes back too. And at one point, state police said searchers had seen a man they believed was Frein somewhere between seventy-five and a hundred yards away through thick woods. They couldn't reach him. Here's something to keep in mind through this next part. When they finally caught him, there was a notebook at that hangar. It's the closest thing we have to hearing what those forty-eight days were like from his side. We'll get to it. On September twenty-ninth, searchers found a campsite. There was clothing, ammunition, Frein's checkbook, and two explosive devices. Bivens described them as fully functional pipe bombs, and he said he believed Frein had left them behind because he was under pressure. The next day, an agent collected a trash bag near the site. Inside were three torn notebook pages describing the attack. That's where the line about taking the shot came from. On October eighth, with Frein still out there, Bivens stood in front of reporters and read from those pages out loud. Then the search went on for three more weeks. By the end, state police put their own cost at about eleven million dollars. That doesn't count what the FBI and the Marshals spent. October thirtieth, day forty-eight. So why were the Marshals at that airfield at all? They weren't following a tip. State police had asked them to clear the abandoned resort, the old Birchwood Pocono Airpark near Tannersville, and they were working through it. Malkowski said afterward, "We just had a hunch that if we were on the run, this is a place we would hide." You know what happened next. The black hat, the order to get down, his name. There's one thing the accounts don't agree on. An early public account said nobody was hurt during the capture, but Frein's face was scraped, and the Marshals themselves said that happened while he was held face down on the pavement. Both versions are on the record, so you're getting both. He wasn't armed in that field. There were weapons inside the hangar, and so was the notebook. This was the longer journal, not the three pages from the trash bag, and it doesn't read like a soldier on a mission. On September twenty-fifth, he wrote that he slept like a human first time in two weeks. On October eleventh, he wrote, "Thirty days. A lot longer than I expected to last." Police also recovered a file on a storage drive. It was a letter addressed Mom and Dad, and in it, he wrote that, "The time seems right for a spark to ignite a fire in the hearts of men." The file had been created on December twenty-ninth, twenty-thirteen, and last accessed on October sixth, twenty-fourteen. Those dates don't tell us when any particular line was written, only when the file was made and when it was last opened. That night, investigators questioned him on video. He called the killing an assassination, and the phrase that came out of that interview was that he'd wanted to wake people up. Back in Barrett Township, the news spread fast. The next day was Halloween, and officials told families that trick-or-treating could go ahead after all. Before we go back to that night, here's how this ended in court. The trial came in April twenty-seventeen in Pike County. Alex Douglas testified. On April nineteenth, the jury convicted Eric Frein on all twelve counts, including first-degree murder of a law enforcement officer and terrorism. Then came the penalty phase to decide whether he'd live. On April twentieth, Brian Dixon's widow, Tiffany Dixon, testified about raising their two sons without their father. Frein's parents testified too, asking for his life. On April twenty-sixth, the jury returned a death verdict. They found no mitigating circumstances. The judge formally imposed the sentence the next day. Remember that recorded statement from the night of the arrest? The jury heard Frein's confession. Two years later, Pennsylvania's highest court said the jury should never have heard it. Frein had repeatedly told investigators he wanted to stop talking. They kept going. The rifle from the hangar fired the bullets that killed Dixon and wounded Douglas. Frein's DNA was on it. The handwriting on the torn pages was his. The court ruled that the confession hadn't changed the verdict. The conviction stood, and so did the death sentence. In January twenty-twenty, the US Supreme Court declined to take the case. Pennsylvania set an execution date for June twenty-second, twenty-twenty. Ten days before it, a Pike County judge put the execution on hold so Frein could continue challenging his conviction and sentence. Pennsylvania hasn't carried out an execution since nineteen ninety-nine. Now go back to October thirtieth, twenty-fourteen. The field, the hangar, the black hat. The US Marshals had made the arrest, but this was a state police case, and the man they'd caught had killed one of their own. So the Marshals handed Eric Frein over to the Pennsylvania State Police, and the troopers who took him put Corporal Brian Dixon's handcuffs on him. Then they put him in Dixon's patrol car and drove him back to Blooming Grove. State Police Commissioner Frank Noonan confirmed it. Pennsylvania's governor at the time, Tom Corbett, called it very appropriate. Forty-eight days after Corporal Brian Dixon was killed outside Blooming Grove, his patrol car pulled back into the barracks. Eric Frein was in the back seat wearing Dixon's handcuffs. So here's my question for you. The state police chose to bring him back in Dixon's handcuffs in Dixon's car. Was that the right call? Tell me what you think in the comments.
